claim: Mice lacking two class I major histocompatibility molecules, MHCI H2-Kb and H2-Db (MHCI KbDb−/−), have enhanced associative long-term depression at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum (PF-Purkinje cell LTD).
source: Previously, we proposed that such learning impairments can result from saturation of the plasticity mechanism (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017), or, more generally, from a history-dependent change in the threshold for plasticity. This hypothesis was based on experimental results from mice lacking two class I major histocompatibility molecules, MHCI H2-Kb and H2-Db (MHCI KbDb−/−), which have enhanced associative long-term depression at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum (PF-Purkinje cell LTD).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017 and references to experimental results from MHCI KbDb−/− mice.

claim: Mice lacking Fmr1 gene expression in cerebellar Purkinje cells (L7-Fmr1 KO) were selectively impaired on two oculomotor learning tasks in which PF-Purkinje cell LTD has been implicated.
source: Mice lacking Fmr1 gene expression in cerebellar Purkinje cells (L7-Fmr1 KO) were selectively impaired on two oculomotor learning tasks in which PF-Purkinje cell LTD has been implicated, with no impairment on LTD-independent oculomotor learning tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing selective impairment in specific oculomotor tasks.

claim: L7-Fmr1 KO mice have no impairment on LTD-independent oculomotor learning tasks.
source: Mice lacking Fmr1 gene expression in cerebellar Purkinje cells (L7-Fmr1 KO) were selectively impaired on two oculomotor learning tasks in which PF-Purkinje cell LTD has been implicated, with no impairment on LTD-independent oculomotor learning tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing normal performance on certain oculomotor tasks.

claim: Behavioral pre-training designed to reverse LTD at the PF-Purkinje cell synapses eliminated the oculomotor learning deficit in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Consistent with the threshold metaplasticity hypothesis, behavioral pre-training designed to reverse LTD at the PF-Purkinje cell synapses eliminated the oculomotor learning deficit in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice, as previously reported in MHCI KbDb−/−mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral pre-training experiments and citation to previous work in MHCI KbDb−/− mice.

claim: Diazepam treatment to suppress neural activity during the pre-training period eliminated the learning deficits in L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: In addition, diazepam treatment to suppress neural activity and thereby limit the induction of associative LTD during the pre-training period also eliminated the learning deficits in L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from diazepam treatment experiments.

claim: Cerebellar LTD-dependent learning is governed by an experience-dependent sliding threshold for plasticity.
source: These results support the hypothesis that cerebellar LTD-dependent learning is governed by an experience-dependent sliding threshold for plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: An increased threshold for LTD in response to elevated neural activity would tend to oppose firing rate stability.
source: An increased threshold for LTD in response to elevated neural activity would tend to oppose firing rate stability, but could serve to stabilize synaptic weights and recently acquired memories.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about the consequences of threshold metaplasticity.

claim: An increased threshold for LTD in response to elevated neural activity could serve to stabilize synaptic weights and recently acquired memories.
source: An increased threshold for LTD in response to elevated neural activity would tend to oppose firing rate stability, but could serve to stabilize synaptic weights and recently acquired memories.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about potential functions of threshold metaplasticity.

claim: Purkinje cell-specific knock out of the Fragile X gene Fmr1 enhances PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: Purkinje cell-specific knock out of the Fragile X gene Fmr1 enhances PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Koekkoek et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Koekkoek et al., 2005.

claim: L7-Fmr1 KO mice are selectively impaired on LTD-dependent oculomotor learning tasks.
source: We show that these L7-Fmr1 KO mice are selectively impaired on LTD-dependent oculomotor learning tasks, and that their learning deficit can be reversed with behavioral pre-training designed to reverse PF-Purkinje cell LTD, as previously reported in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The learning deficit in L7-Fmr1 KO mice can be reversed with behavioral pre-training designed to reverse PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: We show that these L7-Fmr1 KO mice are selectively impaired on LTD-dependent oculomotor learning tasks, and that their learning deficit can be reversed with behavioral pre-training designed to reverse PF-Purkinje cell LTD, as previously reported in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral pre-training experiments.

claim: In some cases, experimental manipulations that augment plasticity have succeeded in augmenting learning.
source: In some cases, experimental manipulations that augment plasticity have succeeded in augmenting learning (Tang et al., 1999; van Praag et al., 1999; Lee and Silva, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tang et al., 1999; van Praag et al., 1999; Lee and Silva, 2009.

claim: In many cases, manipulations that augment plasticity have impaired learning.
source: However, in many cases, manipulations that augment plasticity have impaired learning (Migaud et al., 1998; Uetani et al., 2000; Gu et al., 2002; Cox et al., 2003; Rutten et al., 2008; Navakkode et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Associative LTD at the cerebellar PF-Purkinje cell synapses has been implicated in certain cerebellum-dependent learning tasks and not others.
source: Associative LTD at the cerebellar PF-Purkinje cell synapses (PF-Purkinje cell LTD) has been implicated in certain cerebellum-dependent learning tasks and not others, based in part on the observation of selective learning impairments in mouse lines with impaired PF-Purkinje cell LTD (reviewed in Raymond and Medina, 2018; De Zeeuw et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Double knockout of the major histocompatibility class I molecules MHCI H2-Kb and H2-Db (MHCI KbDb−/−) enhances PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: Contrary to this expectation, double knockout of the major histocompatibility class I molecules MHCI H2-Kb and H2-Db (MHCI KbDb−/−), which enhances PF-Purkinje cell LTD (McConnell et al., 2009), results in the very same, specific oculomotor learning impairment as observed in mice with impaired PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McConnell et al., 2009.

claim: MHCI KbDb−/− mice result in the very same, specific oculomotor learning impairment as observed in mice with impaired PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: Contrary to this expectation, double knockout of the major histocompatibility class I molecules MHCI H2-Kb and H2-Db (MHCI KbDb−/−), which enhances PF-Purkinje cell LTD (McConnell et al., 2009), results in the very same, specific oculomotor learning impairment as observed in mice with impaired PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017.

claim: Enhanced LTD prevents learning by allowing spontaneous activity in the circuit to aberrantly recruit and saturate this form of plasticity, making it unavailable at the specific synapses where it is needed to support learning.
source: To explain the puzzling observation that the enhancement of a plasticity mechanism could yield the same behavioral phenotype as its impairment, we hypothesized that enhanced LTD prevents learning by allowing spontaneous activity in the circuit to aberrantly recruit and saturate this form of plasticity, making it unavailable at the specific synapses where it is needed to support learning.
evidence: The claim represents a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the circuit designed to induce PF-Purkinje cell LTD before training recapitulated in WT mice the same, specific oculomotor learning deficit observed in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced LTD.
source: Two key predictions of this hypothesis were confirmed experimentally by previous work: optogenetic stimulation of the circuit designed to induce PF-Purkinje cell LTD before training recapitulated in WT mice the same, specific oculomotor learning deficit observed in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced LTD; and a behavioral manipulation designed to reverse PF-Purkinje cell LTD before oculomotor training reversed the learning deficit in MHCI KbDb−/− mice (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: A behavioral manipulation designed to reverse PF-Purkinje cell LTD before oculomotor training reversed the learning deficit in MHCI KbDb−/− mice.
source: Two key predictions of this hypothesis were confirmed experimentally by previous work: optogenetic stimulation of the circuit designed to induce PF-Purkinje cell LTD before training recapitulated in WT mice the same, specific oculomotor learning deficit observed in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced LTD; and a behavioral manipulation designed to reverse PF-Purkinje cell LTD before oculomotor training reversed the learning deficit in MHCI KbDb−/− mice (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: VOR-increase training induced an adaptive learned increase in the eye movement responses of wild type (WT) mice to the vestibular stimulus alone.
source: When a vestibular stimulus (1 Hz sinusoidal rotation about an earth-vertical axis with peak velocity of ± 10°/s) was paired with oppositely directed motion of a large-field visual stimulus for 30 min (Figure 1A, left; see Materials and methods), this induced an adaptive learned increase in the eye movement responses of wild type (WT) mice to the vestibular stimulus alone (VOR-increase learning; Figure 1A, right, black; p=7.37 × 10–4, 0 vs 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: VOR-decrease training induced an adaptive learned decrease in the eye movement responses of WT mice to the vestibular stimulus alone.
source: When the vestibular stimulus was instead paired with motion of a visual stimulus in the same direction as the head (Figure 1B, left), this induced an adaptive learned decrease in the eye movement responses of WT mice to the vestibular stimulus alone (VOR-decrease learning; Figure 1B, right, black; p=0.001, 0 vs 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning are cerebellum dependent.
source: Both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning are cerebellum dependent (Ito et al., 1974b; Robinson, 1976; Lisberger et al., 1984; Nagao, 1983; Michnovicz and Bennett, 1987; Pastor et al., 1994; Koekkoek et al., 1997; McElligott et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Manipulations that impair or enhance PF-Purkinje cell LTD have previously been found to selectively alter VOR-increase learning, with less or no effect on VOR-decrease learning.
source: However, manipulations that impair or enhance PF-Purkinje cell LTD have previously been found to selectively alter VOR-increase learning, with less or no effect on VOR-decrease learning (Li et al., 1995; Boyden et al., 2006; Hansel et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2014; Kimpo et al., 2014; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017; Kakegawa et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: L7-Fmr1 KO mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD were selectively and profoundly impaired on VOR-increase learning.
source: Accordingly, the L7-Fmr1 KO mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD were selectively and profoundly impaired on VOR-increase learning. Unlike the WT control group, L7-Fmr1 KO mice exhibited no significant change in the amplitude of their VOR after 30 min of VOR-increase training (Figure 1A, red; p=0.97, L7-Fmr1 KO, 0 vs 30 min; p=3.47 × 10–5, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, 30 min; Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: VOR-decrease learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice was robust and indistinguishable from that of their WT littermates.
source: In contrast, VOR-decrease learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice was robust and indistinguishable from that of their WT littermates (Figure 1B, red; p=1.10 × 10–5, L7-Fmr1 KO, 0 vs 30 min; p=0.091, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, 30 min; Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Baseline oculomotor performance of L7-Fmr1 KO mice was normal.
source: Baseline oculomotor performance of L7-Fmr1 KO mice was normal, as were the eye movement responses to the paired presentation of visual and vestibular stimuli used for both types of training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that there was no deficit in the vestibular, visual or oculomotor functions required to perform the learning tasks; rather the L7-Fmr1 KO mice have a selective deficit in learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The eye movement responses to the paired presentation of visual and vestibular stimuli used for both types of training were normal in L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Baseline oculomotor performance of L7-Fmr1 KO mice was normal, as were the eye movement responses to the paired presentation of visual and vestibular stimuli used for both types of training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that there was no deficit in the vestibular, visual or oculomotor functions required to perform the learning tasks; rather the L7-Fmr1 KO mice have a selective deficit in learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: L7-Fmr1 KO mice have a selective deficit in learning rather than a deficit in the vestibular, visual or oculomotor functions required to perform the learning tasks.
source: Baseline oculomotor performance of L7-Fmr1 KO mice was normal, as were the eye movement responses to the paired presentation of visual and vestibular stimuli used for both types of training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that there was no deficit in the vestibular, visual or oculomotor functions required to perform the learning tasks; rather the L7-Fmr1 KO mice have a selective deficit in learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the normal baseline performance data.

claim: VOR-decrease training can rapidly reverse any behavioral evidence of prior VOR-increase learning in wild-type mice.
source: In wild-type mice, VOR-decrease training can rapidly reverse any behavioral evidence of prior VOR-increase learning, which suggests that VOR-decrease training can reverse any plasticity induced during VOR-increase learning, including any PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Boyden and Raymond, 2003), presumably through the induction of PF-Purkinje cell LTP (Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Shim et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VOR-decrease training can reverse any plasticity induced during VOR-increase learning, including any PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: In wild-type mice, VOR-decrease training can rapidly reverse any behavioral evidence of prior VOR-increase learning, which suggests that VOR-decrease training can reverse any plasticity induced during VOR-increase learning, including any PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Boyden and Raymond, 2003), presumably through the induction of PF-Purkinje cell LTP (Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Shim et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from behavioral observations and supported by citations.

claim: VOR-decrease pre-training was previously found to reverse the oculomotor learning deficit in MHCI KbDb-/- mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: Accordingly, VOR-decrease pre-training was previously found to reverse the oculomotor learning deficit in MHCI KbDb-/- mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: After VOR-decrease pre-training, L7-Fmr1 KO mice exhibited VOR-increase learning indistinguishable from WT.
source: Although in the absence of pre-training, VOR-increase training failed to induce any significant change in the VOR of the L7-Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 2A, red, solid lines and bar graph; p=0.99, L7-Fmr1 KO, 0 vs 30 min, Tukey), the same VOR-increase training procedure did induce a significant increase in VOR amplitude when delivered to the same cohort of mice after VOR-decrease pre-training (Figure 2B, red, solid lines and bar graph, p=0.001, 0 vs 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ability of the L7-Fmr1 KO mice to learn in response to the VOR-increase training varied with the recent history of experience.
source: In other words, the ability of the L7-Fmr1 KO mice to learn in response to the VOR-increase training varied with the recent history of experience (Figure 2, compare red bars in A vs. B; p=0.01, VOR-increase learning of L7-Fmr1 KO without vs. with pre-training, paired sample t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis comparing conditions shown in Figure 2.

claim: The amount of learning exhibited by WT mice in response to VOR-increase training was not enhanced after VOR-decrease pre-training.
source: Pre-training experience did not have the same effect in WT mice. The amount of learning exhibited by WT mice in response to VOR-increase training was not enhanced after VOR-decrease pre-training (Figure 2, compare black bars in A vs.B; p=0.41, paired sample t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: VOR-decrease pre-training had different effects on the L7-Fmr1 KO and WT mice, putting the L7-Fmr1 KO mice, but not the WT mice, into a state more compatible with VOR-increase learning.
source: Thus, VOR-decrease pre-training had different effects on the L7-Fmr1 KO and WT mice, putting the L7-Fmr1 KO mice, but not the WT mice, into a state more compatible with VOR-increase learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential effects of pre-training on the two genotypes.

claim: After thirty minutes of Vestibular only pre-training, subsequent VOR-increase learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice was comparable to that of their WT littermates.
source: A second behavioral pre-training procedure, habituation of the VOR, induced by presentation of the vestibular stimulus alone in complete darkness (Vestibular only pre-training), had effects similar to those of VOR-decrease pre-training on subsequent VOR-increase learning. After thirty minutes of Vestibular only pre-training, subsequent VOR-increase learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice was comparable to that of their WT littermates (Figure 2C, red vs. black bars; p=0.84, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, VOR-increase from 0 to 30 min, t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PF-Purkinje cell LTD is driven by co-activation of cerebellar parallel fibers and climbing fibers.
source: Since PF-Purkinje cell LTD is driven by co-activation of cerebellar parallel fibers and climbing fibers (Ito and Kano, 1982; Ito, 1982; Linden and Connor, 1995), pharmacological suppression of neural activity should also prevent the induction and increase in the threshold for LTD during the pre-training period, and restore the capacity for subsequent LTD-dependent learning in mice with enhanced LTD.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Diazepam is a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors.
source: We tested this prediction by administering the benzodiazepine diazepam, a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors, to enhance inhibition and suppress neural activity in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice during the period preceding VOR-increase training.
evidence: The claim is based on established pharmacological knowledge about diazepam.

claim: Diazepam has been shown to reduce neural firing in cerebellar neurons and neural responses to vestibular stimuli.
source: Diazepam has been shown to reduce neural firing in cerebellar neurons and neural responses to vestibular stimuli (Ryu and McCabe, 1974; Barmack and Pettorossi, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The acute effect of diazepam administration was to impair learning.
source: The acute effect of diazepam administration was to impair learning. There was no effect of diazepam on the baseline amplitude of the VOR response measured in the dark 2 hr after diazepam (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), contrary to what has been reported in rabbit (Barmack and Pettorossi, 1980). However, when VOR-increase training was delivered 2 hr after systemic administration of diazepam, VOR-increase learning was profoundly impaired in WT as well as L7-Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Diazepam has a long half-life of ~24 hr.
source: Diazepam has a long half-life of ~24 hr (Riss et al., 2008), therefore mice were allowed to recover in their home cage for 18–24 hr after diazepam administration, and then VOR learning was tested after recovery from this prolonged period of pharmacological suppression of neural activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Riss et al., 2008.

claim: 18-24 hours after diazepam administration, the L7-Fmr1 KO mice exhibited robust VOR-increase learning, comparable to their WT littermates.
source: Remarkably, the L7-Fmr1 KO mice exhibited robust VOR-increase learning, comparable to their WT littermates (Figure 3B, top, red vs. black; p=0.86, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Diazepam pre-treatment eliminated the VOR-increase learning deficit in L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Although the same individual L7-Fmr1 KO had exhibited no significant learning in response to VOR-increase training in the absence of the pharmacological pre-treatment (p=0.99, 0 vs 30 min, data for subset of mice in Figure 1A used in Figure 3 experiments, Tukey), diazepam pre-treatment eliminated this learning deficit.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing learning with and without diazepam pre-treatment.

claim: The enhancement of learning by diazepam pre-treatment was temporary.
source: The enhancement of learning by diazepam pre-treatment was temporary. When the same mice were re-tested one week after diazepam administration, the L7-Fmr1 KO mice again failed to learn in response to VOR-increase training (Figure 3C, red; p=0.12, 0 vs 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Diazepam pre-treatment could restore the VOR circuit of L7-Fmr1 KO mice to a state compatible with VOR-increase learning, but this effect was transient.
source: Thus, diazepam pre-treatment could restore the VOR circuit of L7-Fmr1 KO mice to a state compatible with VOR-increase learning, but this effect was transient.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the temporary nature of the diazepam effect.

claim: Wild type mice did not exhibit enhanced VOR-increase learning after diazepam pre-treatment.
source: Wild type mice did not exhibit enhanced VOR-increase learning after diazepam pre-treatment (Figure 3B top vs. Figure 2A, black, p=0.55; Figure 3B vs. 3 C, top, black, p=0.99; paired sample t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis comparing conditions.

claim: There was no effect of diazepam pre-treatment on VOR-decrease learning in either the WT or L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Moreover, there was no effect of diazepam pre-treatment on VOR-decrease learning in either the WT or L7-Fmr1 KO mice (compare Figure 3B, bottom vs. Figure 1B; p=0.91, WT, 1 day post-diazepam vs. control, VOR-decrease at 30 min, paired sample t-test; p=0.37, L7-Fmr1 KO, 1 day post-diazepam vs. control, VOR-decrease at 30 min, paired sample t-test; p=0.11, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT 1 day post-diazepam, VOR-decrease at 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis comparing conditions.

claim: Both the learning impairment in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice and the effects of diazepam pre-treatment were selective for VOR-increase learning.
source: Thus, both the learning impairment in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice and the effects of diazepam pre-treatment were selective for VOR-increase learning, consistent with previous evidence that this form of VOR learning is more dependent on PF-Purkinje cell LTD than VOR-decrease learning (Li et al., 1995; Boyden et al., 2006; Hansel et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2014; Kimpo et al., 2014; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017; Kakegawa et al., 2018; Jang et al., 2020; Shim et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the selective effects observed and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous work has suggested a selective contribution of PF-Purkinje cell LTD to VOR learning induced with high-frequency (≥1 Hz) vestibular and visual stimuli, with less contribution of LTD when VOR learning is induced with low-frequency (≤0.66 Hz) vestibular and visual stimuli.
source: Previous work has also suggested a selective contribution of PF-Purkinje cell LTD to VOR learning induced with high-frequency (≥1 Hz) vestibular and visual stimuli, with less contribution of LTD when VOR learning is induced with low-frequency (≤0.66 Hz) vestibular and visual stimuli (Boyden et al., 2006; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There was a trend for low-frequency (0.5 Hz) as well as high-frequency (1 Hz) VOR-increase learning to be impaired in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We found a trend for low-frequency (0.5 Hz, Figure 4) as well as high-frequency (1 Hz, Figures 1—3) VOR-increase learning to be impaired in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 4A, left, red vs. black; p=0.06, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, 30 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The low-frequency learning impairment was not reversed by the pre-training procedures that reversed the high-frequency learning impairment.
source: However, the low-frequency learning impairment was not reversed by the pre-training procedures that reversed the high-frequency learning impairment. Neither behavioral pre-training (Figure 4A, red, middle, p=0.47, L7-Fmr1 KO, VOR-decrease Pre-training vs. no Pre-training; right, p=0.35, L7-Fmr1 KO, Vestibular only Pre-training vs. no Pre-training; paired sample t-test), nor treatment with diazepam 18–24 hr before training (Figure 4B, compare red bars; p=0.66, L7-Fmr1 KO, saline vs. diazepam, paired sample t-test), reversed the impairment of low-frequency VOR-increase learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice, in contrast to their effectiveness at reversing the impairment of high-frequency VOR-increase learning (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The behavioral and pharmacological pre-training manipulations selectively restore the capacity for learning tasks that depend on PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that the behavioral and pharmacological pre-training manipulations selectively restore the capacity for learning tasks that depend on PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the selective effects of pre-training on different learning tasks.

claim: OKR adaptation is the oculomotor learning task for which there is arguably the strongest evidence for a critical role of PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: To further test the specificity of the effects of Fmr1 knockout and diazepam pre-treatment for learning tasks that depend on PF-Purkinje cell LTD, we tested optokinetic reflex (OKR) adaption, which is the oculomotor learning task for which there is arguably the strongest evidence for a critical role of PF-Purkinje cell LTD (Takeuchi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014; Inoshita and Hirano, 2018; Kakegawa et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In WT mice, 60 min of training with the optokinetic stimulus induced a learned increase in the amplitude of the OKR response.
source: In WT mice, 60 min of training with the optokinetic stimulus induced a learned increase in the amplitude of the OKR response, as the mice learned to more closely match their eye movements to the motion of the optokinetic stimulus and thus improve stability of its image on the retina (Figure 5A, black, p=0.001, 0 vs 60 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The L7-Fmr1 KO mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD had significantly impaired OKR adaptation.
source: The L7-Fmr1 KO mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD had significantly impaired OKR adaptation (Figure 5A, red vs. black; p=1.27 × 10–4, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, 60 min; p=0.87, L7-Fmr1 KO, 0 vs 60 min; Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The OKR adaptation learning deficit in L7-Fmr1 KO mice was completely eliminated by pre-treatment with diazepam 18–24 hr before training.
source: This learning deficit was completely eliminated by pre-treatment with diazepam 18–24 hr before training (Figure 5B). Indeed, the L7-Fmr1 KO mice not only learned better 18–24 hr after diazepam than they did without this pre-treatment (Compare Figure 5A vs. B, red; p=0.0001, saline vs. diazepam pre-treatment, 60 min, Tukey), but their learning after diazepam pre-treatment was even enhanced relative to WT (Figure 5B, red vs. black; p=0.02, L7-Fmr1 KO vs. WT, 60 min, Tukey).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In both the L7-Fmr1 KO and MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD, the learning impairments and the enhancement of learning by behavioral or pharmacological pre-training manipulations were remarkably selective for the oculomotor learning tasks in which PF-Purkinje cell LTD has been most strongly implicated.
source: In both the L7-Fmr1 KO and MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced PF-Purkinje cell LTD, the learning impairments and the enhancement of learning by behavioral or pharmacological pre-training manipulations were remarkably selective for the oculomotor learning tasks in which PF-Purkinje cell LTD has been most strongly implicated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern of selective effects observed across multiple experiments.

claim: Both lines of mice (L7-Fmr1 KO and MHCI KbDb−/−) were profoundly impaired on high-frequency VOR-increase learning and OKR adaptation.
source: Both lines of mice were profoundly impaired on high-frequency VOR-increase learning and OKR adaptation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both mouse lines.

claim: Pre-training only enhanced learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO and MHCI KbDb−/− mice, and not WT mice.
source: Moreover, pre-training only enhanced learning in the L7-Fmr1 KO and MHCI KbDb−/− mice, and not WT mice, consistent with the pre-training selectively reversing limitations caused by enhanced LTD, rather than generally enhancing cerebellum-dependent learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of pre-training on different genotypes.

claim: The deletion of Fmr1 from Purkinje cells may have two distinct effects: enhancement of PF-Purkinje cell LTD, which recapitulates the high-frequency VOR-increase learning phenotypes observed in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced LTD, plus disruption of an additional cellular mechanism that contributes to low-frequency VOR-increase learning.
source: In other words, the deletion of Fmr1 from Purkinje cells may have two distinct effects: enhancement of PF-Purkinje cell LTD, which recapitulates the high-frequency VOR-increase learning phenotypes observed in the MHCI KbDb−/− mice with enhanced LTD, plus disruption of an additional cellular mechanism that contributes to low-frequency VOR-increase learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential effects of pre-training on high- vs. low-frequency learning.

claim: The very similar behavioral phenotypes observed when PF-Purkinje cell LTD is enhanced by manipulating different molecular cascades strengthens the evidence that their shared effect of enhancing LTD is responsible for their shared learning impairments.
source: The very similar behavioral phenotypes observed when PF-Purkinje cell LTD is enhanced by manipulating different molecular cascades further strengthens the evidence that their shared effect of enhancing LTD is responsible for their shared learning impairments, rather than other, off-target effects of the molecular manipulations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the convergence of phenotypes across different genetic manipulations.

claim: MHCI H2-Db acts on MAP kinase and integrin via interaction with immune receptors such as PirB.
source: MHCI H2- Db acts on MAP kinase and integrin via interaction with immune receptors such as PirB (Shatz, 2009), whereas Fmr1 acts by inhibiting mGluR-dependent dendritic protein translation (Huber et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shatz, 2009.

claim: Fmr1 acts by inhibiting mGluR-dependent dendritic protein translation.
source: MHCI H2- Db acts on MAP kinase and integrin via interaction with immune receptors such as PirB (Shatz, 2009), whereas Fmr1 acts by inhibiting mGluR-dependent dendritic protein translation (Huber et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huber et al., 2002.

claim: Loss of MHCI H2-Db or Fmr1 expression from the Purkinje cells yields enhancement of PF-Purkinje cell LTD.
source: Each yields enhancement of PF-Purkinje cell LTD, as measured by the ability of protocols that fail to induce LTD in slices from WT mice to induce LTD in slices from MHCI KbDb−/− (McConnell et al., 2009) and L7-Fmr1 KO mice (Koekkoek et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pre-treatment with the FDA-approved drug diazepam restored the capacity for high-frequency VOR-increase learning and OKR adaptation in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice without compromising other forms of oculomotor learning or baseline oculomotor performance.
source: Pre-treatment with the FDA-approved drug diazepam restored the capacity for high-frequency VOR-increase learning and OKR adaptation in the L7-Fmr1 KO mice without compromising other forms of oculomotor learning or baseline oculomotor performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing selective restoration of learning without side effects.

claim: Diazepam pre-treatment fully rescued the learning impairments with no apparent side effects on other, closely related functions of the same neural circuitry.
source: This was true even for VOR-decrease learning, which may depend on LTP of the same population of PF-Purkinje cell synapses that undergo LTD during VOR-increase learning (Shim et al., 2022). In other words, diazepam pre-treatment fully rescued the learning impairments with no apparent side effects on other, closely related functions of the same neural circuitry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the selective effects of diazepam pre-treatment.

claim: Pharmacological suppression of neural activity should suppress PF-Purkinje cell LTD throughout the cerebellum, and hence may have the general effect of restoring all regions of the cerebellum to a state compatible with new LTD-dependent learning.
source: Pharmacological suppression of neural activity should suppress PF-Purkinje cell LTD throughout the cerebellum, and hence may have the general effect of restoring all regions of the cerebellum to a state compatible with new LTD-dependent learning.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the potential generality of the pharmacological approach.

claim: The approach of limiting neural activity during a period before training to reset elevated thresholds for plasticity may be broadly applicable throughout the brain for resetting neural circuits to a state compatible with adaptive plasticity and new learning.
source: Thus, the approach of limiting neural activity during a period before training to reset elevated thresholds for plasticity may be broadly applicable throughout the brain for resetting neural circuits to a state compatible with adaptive plasticity and new learning.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the potential broad applicability of the approach.

claim: Suppression of neural activity in the retina has been successfully employed to reset the visual circuitry and enable recovery from amblyopia in adult mice and cats.
source: Consistent with this, suppression of neural activity in the retina has been successfully employed to reset the visual circuitry and enable recovery from amblyopia in adult mice and cats (Fong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fong et al., 2021.

claim: Threshold metaplasticity has not been directly documented at PF-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: The results predict history-dependent changes in the availability of PF-Purkinje cell LTD to support learning due to activity-dependent changes in the threshold for LTD. Threshold metaplasticity has not been directly documented at these synapses, however several factors that influence climbing fiber-induced calcium influx or the probability of LTD induction have been identified (reviewed in Zang and De Schutter, 2019), which could provide the mechanistic substrate for threshold metaplasticity.
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement about the current state of evidence.

claim: Several factors that influence climbing fiber-induced calcium influx or the probability of LTD induction have been identified, which could provide the mechanistic substrate for threshold metaplasticity.
source: Threshold metaplasticity has not been directly documented at these synapses, however several factors that influence climbing fiber-induced calcium influx or the probability of LTD induction have been identified (reviewed in Zang and De Schutter, 2019), which could provide the mechanistic substrate for threshold metaplasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous studies and supported by citation to a review.

claim: The concept of experience-dependent changes in the threshold for synaptic plasticity has been highly influential in theoretical and computational neuroscience.
source: The concept of experience-dependent changes in the threshold for synaptic plasticity has been highly influential in theoretical and computational neuroscience (Abraham and Bear, 1996; Benusková et al., 1999; Cooper and Bear, 2012; Hulme et al., 2012; Lee, 2022), since the foundational work of Bienenstock et al., 1982.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple theoretical and computational studies.

claim: Experimental evidence for whether and how threshold metaplasticity supports the function of neural circuits has been limited.
source: However, experimental evidence for whether and how such threshold metaplasticity supports the function of neural circuits has been limited, and derived largely from studies of the effects of sensory deprivation on the functional connectivity of circuits (Mioche and Singer, 1989; Kirkwood et al., 1996; Philpot et al., 2003; He et al., 2007; Yee et al., 2017) rather than studies of learning per se.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents an assessment of the current state of evidence.

claim: An increased threshold for LTP in response to an increase in neural activity would counter the instability inherent in Hebbian LTP and provide a mechanism to stabilize firing rates and synaptic weights within a desired range.
source: A sliding threshold for plasticity has been conceived as a mechanism for countering an instability inherent in Hebbian LTP whereby correlated pre- and post-synaptic activity strengthens a synapse, which leads to an increase in correlated activity, which in turn leads to further strengthening. An increased threshold for LTP in response to an increase in neural activity would counter this instability and provide a mechanism to stabilize firing rates and synaptic weights within a desired range (van Rossum et al., 2000; Toyoizumi et al., 2014; Yger and Gilson, 2015; Zenke et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Plasticity at the cerebellar PF-Purkinje cell synapse is described as 'anti-Hebbian' because the associative form of plasticity is LTD.
source: In contrast, plasticity at the cerebellar PF-Purkinje cell synapse is described as 'anti-Hebbian' because the associative form of plasticity is LTD.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the nature of plasticity at these synapses.

claim: Associative LTD lacks the instability inherent in Hebbian LTP.
source: Associative LTD lacks the instability inherent in Hebbian LTP.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about the properties of different forms of plasticity.

claim: An increased threshold for LTD in response to an increase in neural activity would tend to oppose rather than support the stability of firing rates of the postsynaptic Purkinje cells.
source: Moreover, an increased threshold for LTD in response to an increase in neural activity or a decreased threshold for LTD in response to decreased neural activity would tend to oppose rather than support the stability of firing rates of the postsynaptic Purkinje cells.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about the consequences of threshold metaplasticity for anti-Hebbian plasticity.

claim: Rather than supporting homeostatic control of firing rates, the central function of threshold metaplasticity at PF-Purkinje cell synapses may be to limit the amount of plasticity.
source: Thus, rather than supporting homeostatic control of firing rates, the central function of threshold metaplasticity at these synapses may be to limit the amount of plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the function of threshold metaplasticity at these synapses.

claim: Manipulations of neural activity during the pre-training period had different effects in the mice with enhanced LTD than in WT mice.
source: In addition, the finding that manipulations of neural activity during the pre-training period had different effects in the mice with enhanced LTD than in WT mice suggests that changes in the threshold for plasticity may be driven, not directly by firing rates, but by the recent history of activity-dependent induction of plasticity (Montgomery and Madison, 2002; Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Hunley et al., 2023; Abraham, 2008; Martin and Kosik, 2002; Redondo and Morris, 2011)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential effects of pre-training and supported by citations.

claim: A plasticity-driven increase in the threshold for further plasticity could serve to protect newly acquired memories from being overwritten.
source: A plasticity-driven increase in the threshold for further plasticity could serve to protect newly acquired memories from being overwritten (Fusi et al., 2005; Benna and Fusi, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential functions supported by citations.

claim: A second potential function of threshold metaplasticity would be to separate memories acquired in close succession onto the synapses of different Purkinje cells.
source: A second potential function would be to separate memories acquired in close succession onto the synapses of different Purkinje cells, in contrast to findings in the amygdala, where there is evidence that a plasticity-driven decrease in the threshold for further plasticity supports the allocation of memories acquired in close succession to the same neurons (Han et al., 2007; Benna and Fusi, 2016; Cai et al., 2016; Rashid et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential functions supported by citations to work in other brain regions.

claim: A lower threshold for synaptic plasticity can result in its aberrant recruitment by ongoing activity in a circuit, resulting in an increased threshold for its subsequent induction and hence the impairment of learning.
source: The current results, along with the previous work by Nguyen-Vu et al., 2017, provide convergent evidence that a lower threshold for synaptic plasticity can result in its aberrant recruitment by ongoing activity in a circuit, resulting in an increased threshold for its subsequent induction and hence the impairment of learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current and previous experimental results.

claim: Learning deficits associated with abnormal plasticity are not necessarily permanent, but in some cases can be remedied with appropriate reset of the circuit.
source: The implication is that learning deficits associated with abnormal plasticity are not necessarily permanent, but in some cases can be remedied with appropriate reset of the circuit, opening up the possibility for therapeutic approaches targeting neural activity as well as the plasticity mechanisms themselves.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing reversibility of learning deficits.

claim: Purkinje-cell-specific Fmr1 knock out mice were generated by crossing conditional Fmr1 knockout mice with mice expressing Cre under the control of the L7/Pcp2 promoter.
source: Purkinje-cell-specific Fmr1 knock out mice were generated by crossing conditional Fmr1 knockout mice (Mientjes et al., 2006) with mice expressing Cre under the control of the L7/Pcp2 promoter (Zhang et al., 2004; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used and is supported by citations.

claim: The L7/Pcp2-Cre Jdhu line expresses Cre-recombinase in a manner that is highly selective for Purkinje cells.
source: The L7/Pcp2-Cre Jdhu line expresses Cre-recombinase in a manner that is highly selective for Purkinje cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the L7/Pcp2-Cre line.

claim: Similar learning deficits were observed in male and female L7-Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Similar learning deficits were observed in male and female L7-Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), therefore results were pooled across sex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The VOR stabilizes images on the retina by using the vestibular sensory input caused by a head movement to drive an oppositely directed eye movement response.
source: The VOR stabilizes images on the retina by using the vestibular sensory input caused by a head movement to drive an oppositely directed eye movement response.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the VOR.

claim: Learning can adjust the amplitude of the VOR to improve the stabilization of visual images on the retina for successful navigation in the world.
source: Learning can adjust the amplitude of this oculomotor reflex to improve the stabilization of visual images on the retina for successful navigation in the world (Gonshor and Jones, 1973; Ito et al., 1974a; Miles and Fuller, 1974; Broussard and Kassardjian, 2004; Gittis and du Lac, 2006; Cullen, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.
